title: Swing Vote

jokes.text: I'm guessing it's my latest budget cut proposal based on your rage sweat.
jokes.setup: Leslie bursts in angrily saying 'What the hell is this?'
jokes.punchline: Ron calmly deduces it's his budget cut proposal from her 'rage sweat' — deadpan diagnosis of her emotional state
jokes.explanation: Sharp cold open. 'Rage sweat' is a great coinage — specific, slightly clinical, and perfectly Ron. The deadpan confidence of 'I'm guessing' makes it land. High character integration because only Ron would analyze Leslie's physical symptoms dispassionately. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm glowing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're sweating. You're sweating through your shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I prefer to think of it as glowing.

jokes.text: First of all, I am rage glowing. Second, you wanna cut funding for the Pawnee Palms Public Putt-Putt? What did the P.P.P.P.P. ever do to you?
jokes.setup: Ron accuses her of rage sweat
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects 'rage sweat' to 'rage glowing' (vanity-driven distinction), then the absurd string of P's in the acronym
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one: the 'rage glowing' correction is perfectly Leslie (she'd never admit to sweating), and the P.P.P.P.P. acronym absurdity is a good Parks visual/verbal gag. The character specificity is excellent — Leslie's civic pride and vanity collide.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're not cutting funding for Pawnee Palms Public Putt-Putt. We're just going to call it something else. Pawnee Parks and Public Programming Proposal. P-P-P-P-P.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'I believe in cutting useless government projects. I also believe in cutting useful projects, future projects, and past projects. The Hoover Dam is a travesty.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains his anti-government philosophy regarding the mini-golf cut
jokes.punchline: The escalating list (useless → useful → future → past) culminates in the Hoover Dam being a travesty — absurdist extremity that's perfectly Ron
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation structure is impeccable — useless to useful to future to PAST projects is a brilliant logical progression that exposes Ron's ideology as self-parody. The Hoover Dam as a specific, iconic example is perfectly chosen. Highly quotable. This is what Ron Swanson character comedy looks like at its best — the joke couldn't exist outside this character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We cannot cut funding for police, fire, and emergency services. We also cannot cut funding for the city's prized collection of decorative urns, or the department that organizes our annual Sweetcorn Festival, or Jerry's salary. Whatever.

jokes.text: You also believe in making furniture. Why don't you go solder a chair instead?
jokes.setup: Ron has just finished his anti-government manifesto
jokes.punchline: Leslie pivots to Ron's woodworking hobby with 'solder a chair' — deliberately using the wrong craftsmanship term to mock him
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Leslie knows Ron makes furniture but says 'solder' (electronics term) rather than 'build' or 'carve,' either as a deliberate dig or genuine ignorance. Either reading is funny. Good character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I believe in small government. Very small government. So small that it's barely there at all.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No taxes, no regulations, no bureaucracy. Just people, doing what they want, when they want.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: In fact, I'm so opposed to government that I think we should abolish all the roads. They were built by the government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: We should tear up all the highways, all the interstates. Also, the Golden Gate Bridge? Gone. Mount Rushmore? Dynamite.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The Hoover Dam was built by the government, so that's coming down. And honestly, the government created gravity, so I'm working on removing that too.

jokes.text: Do you expect me to make a chair out of transistor chips and small wires?
jokes.setup: Leslie tells him to 'solder a chair'
jokes.punchline: Ron takes the malapropism literally and deadpans the logical conclusion — he'd need to make a chair out of electronic components
jokes.explanation: Ron playing it completely straight — not correcting Leslie but instead pointing out the absurd material implications — is perfect. The joke rewards the viewer who clocked 'solder' as the wrong word. Clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, instead of cutting the budget, why don't you go build something? Use your woodworking skills.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand. What am I building? You said 'use your skills' but you're holding a computer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If I'm supposed to build something, I need wood, not... whatever this is.

jokes.text: That putt-putt is gonna be around forever, and when I am done with it, it'll attract more visitors than the Hoover Dam.
jokes.setup: Leslie vows to fight for the mini-golf course
jokes.punchline: Comparing a local putt-putt to the Hoover Dam in visitor numbers — absurdly grandiose civic pride
jokes.explanation: The Hoover Dam callback from joke 3 elevates this — Leslie unconsciously picks Ron's own reference point to make her case. Classic Parks absurdity from Leslie's overblown civic pride.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The putt-putt golf course will produce more electricity than the Hoover Dam.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, how is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't have a plan yet, but I'm thinking decorative windmills.

jokes.text: And it'll produce double the amount of electricity. / How? / I'll figure it out. / It already has windmills. Who cares?
jokes.setup: Leslie claims the putt-putt will outdo the Hoover Dam in visitors
jokes.punchline: She escalates to claiming it'll produce double the electricity; when challenged, she says 'I'll figure it out' — and Ron's dry 'It already has windmills. Who cares?' is the cap
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation. Leslie's 'I'll figure it out' is confident Leslie at her most delusional-optimistic. Ron's capper 'It already has windmills. Who cares?' is brilliant — completely deflating, weirdly accurate, and delivered with total indifference. The whole mini-exchange is tightly constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You both look so handsome today.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Why thank you, Leslie. I do take pride in my appearance.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: I think I'm going to be sick.

jokes.text: Councilmen, I have something to discuss with you, but before I do, can I just point out how handsome the both of you look today? / Yeah, I know. / I feel very ill.
jokes.setup: Leslie opens with flattery toward the two councilmen
jokes.punchline: Jamm accepts the compliment with total self-satisfaction; Milton reports he feels ill — both responses subvert the expected 'thank you'
jokes.explanation: The double subversion works well. Jamm's narcissistic 'Yeah, I know' and Milton's non-sequitur illness are both in character and funny in different directions. Milton's 'I feel very ill' as a response to being called handsome is particularly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: I think mini-golf is a wonderful activity. It brings people together, it's fun for the whole family...

dialogue.speaker: Milton
dialogue.line: But I have to be honest, I can't support it. You see, mini-golf courses have holes in them. And I don't think we should be encouraging anything with holes.

jokes.text: Well, the last time I was there, I saw kids of all races getting along and playing. [beat] It was terrible. So I'm voting to get rid of it.
jokes.setup: Milton says he saw kids of all races getting along — sounds like a heartwarming endorsement
jokes.punchline: 'It was terrible.' The pause before the reversal is the structural heart of the joke — he finds racial harmony at a putt-putt objectionable
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's sharpest jokes. The structural beat — the pause after 'getting along and playing' — does enormous work. The audience is lulled into expecting a positive conclusion, and the reversal ('It was terrible') lands like a thunderclap. The brevity is perfect. Milton's racism is established character comedy, but the misdirection structure here elevates it well above a simple character gag. The economy is exceptional — four words ('It was terrible') deliver a complete political and comedic payload.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Well, let me weigh the pros and cons here.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: On one hand, it's the right thing to do. On the other hand, I don't want to. On the third hand, I really hate Leslie.

jokes.text: At least you have a good reason.
jokes.setup: Milton has just said he's voting against the course because he saw racial integration there
jokes.punchline: Leslie says 'At least you have a good reason' with clear sarcasm — a perfectly calibrated reaction to an outrageous statement
jokes.explanation: Great reaction beat and a perfect one-liner. Leslie's sarcasm is restrained and effective — she doesn't over-explain the horror of what Milton said, which is the right comedy instinct. Economy is the strength here.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm a badass wild card. Nobody knows how I'm going to vote.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: It keeps people on their toes.

jokes.text: Well, on the one hand, I love cutting government programs. On the other hand, mini-golf rules. And on the third hand, I hate both you and Ron Swanson. So this one could go either way. I'm kind of a badass wild card.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Jamm which way he's leaning on the vote
jokes.punchline: He lists three 'hands' (absurdist structure), with the third hand being 'I hate you both' as a legitimate factor, and caps with self-aggrandizing 'badass wild card'
jokes.explanation: The 'third hand' escalation is a strong structural choice — it signals Jamm's complete irrationality as a politician. 'I'm kind of a badass wild card' as sincere self-description is perfect Jamm: delusional, petty, and self-important. The joke earns laughs through character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: I'm a very sexually active man. Women find me irresistible.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm not doing anyone right now and I'm completely available.

jokes.text: Hey, what are you doing tonight? / More like who am I doing? [beat] No one. I'm free. What's up?
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Jamm what he's doing tonight
jokes.punchline: Jamm's instinctive sexual brag, followed immediately by the deflating '...No one. I'm free.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed two-beat joke. Jamm's instinct is to brag sexually, but reality immediately deflates it. The pause between 'No one' and 'I'm free' is crucial — it transforms Jamm from sleazy to pathetic in an instant. The economy of the reversal is excellent. This encapsulates Jamm as a character: aspires to be a cool villain, actually a lonely dork.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you designated me as the driver? You're driving right now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I ordered water. Once you order water, you're committed to the car for the entire ride.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's the rules, Ben. I don't make them.

jokes.text: Nah, it's too late, bro. I already ordered the water.
jokes.setup: Ben points out that Andy drove there, so he can't be the designated driver
jokes.punchline: Andy's logic: the order has been placed, therefore the role is locked in. The 'bro' makes it worse/better.
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete non-logic delivered as absolute fact is a great character beat. 'Too late, bro' as a response to a factual correction shows Andy operating by his own internal ruleset. Tight economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've been taken advantage of so many times. My first girlfriend made me carry all her books. My college roommate ate my food without asking. My boss at my first job made me work weekends.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you really need to be more assertive.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're right. Starting now, I'm going to stand up for myself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Great! So what's your first step?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I was thinking...

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: 'And somehow I just ended up becoming the designated driver. And paying for everyone. And I didn't get to choose the bar. I should be more assertive.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains how the celebratory outing was organized
jokes.punchline: Each new revelation is worse (designated driver → paying → no bar choice), ending with the meek self-diagnosis 'I should be more assertive'
jokes.explanation: Classic escalating confessional structure. The pauses between each new indignity work well in mockumentary format. Ben's gentle self-awareness ('I should be more assertive') is perfectly characterful — he sees the problem but lacks the fire to fix it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You guys sound great!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, like a CD that got stuck in your car and plays the same five songs over and over.

jokes.text: Really? They sound kinda crappy to me. / Kinda sounds like one of your songs, babe.
jokes.setup: April says the bar band is good tonight; Tom and Mona-Lisa react
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa casually insults the band, then Tom notes it sounds like one of Andy's songs — which is either a compliment or an insult
jokes.explanation: Sets up the Mouse Rat subplot efficiently. The humor is mild — Mona-Lisa's blunt rudeness and Tom's inadvertent insult. Functional setup comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, that's my band! Why didn't I recognize them? Oh, I know why — because I'm not in it, so my brain filtered it out as irrelevant.

jokes.text: That's my band. I didn't recognize us without me because I'm the only one that matters.
jokes.setup: Andy realizes the bar band is playing a Mouse Rat song
jokes.punchline: His narcissistic explanation: he couldn't identify his own band because he himself was absent — and he's the only element that matters
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy line. The logic is childishly solipsistic and completely sincere — he's not being mean, he genuinely believes it. 'I didn't recognize us without me' is a great construction. Perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What about 'Rat Mouse'?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's just Mouse Rat backwards.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Thank you, everyone. We are Rat Mouse.
jokes.setup: The band finishes the Mouse Rat song
jokes.punchline: They've renamed themselves 'Rat Mouse' — not even a creative rebrand, just the words flipped
jokes.explanation: The name 'Rat Mouse' is perfectly stupid — it shows the band couldn't be bothered to even pretend to start fresh. It's funny because it's simultaneously petty and lazy. 'Mouse Rat' is already a famously absurd band name, so the inversion is a meta-joke for established Parks fans.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Hey Tom, can I borrow your car for like six months?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Six months? No, absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Well, too late. I already have it. And I lost it.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Why are you always interrogating me?

jokes.text: Rat bastards. They're playing without me?
jokes.setup: Andy sees 'Rat Mouse' performing his band's song
jokes.punchline: 'Rat bastards' is both a genuine expletive and a pun on 'Rat Mouse' — deliberate or accidental from Andy, it doesn't matter
jokes.explanation: The accidental/intentional pun works beautifully. Whether Andy means it as wordplay doesn't matter — the audience gets it. Economy is perfect: three words carry outrage, betrayal, and wit simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I once ate a whole rotisserie chicken in a bathroom stall at the mall. But hey, you seem like a cool guy — you wanna go back to my place and make out?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Hey, baby, can I borrow your car for a month? / I already lent you my car. / Do you not know where my car is? / Ugh, I'm so sick of the third degree. It's like dating a cop.
jokes.setup: Tom asks to borrow Mona-Lisa's car
jokes.punchline: It turns out she already lent him her car and he doesn't know where it is — and Mona-Lisa's response is to call the basic question 'the third degree'
jokes.explanation: Rapid-fire chaos establishing Mona-Lisa's insanity. The inversion — Mona-Lisa calling a totally reasonable question 'the third degree' — effectively characterizes her. 'It's like dating a cop' is a nice line.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Dating Mona-Lisa is awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm in constant fear for my life.

jokes.text: I'm gassy. Let's make out.
jokes.setup: Tom is confronting Mona-Lisa about his car
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa completely derails the conversation with a non-sequitur gas/makeout proposal
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly capture Mona-Lisa. The combination of a gross bodily disclosure with a romantic proposition, delivered as a single sentence, is inspired. The absolute economy (10/10) is the joke — there's no wasted syllable. Highly quotable and shocking enough to get a big room reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, my girlfriend is crazy. Can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not crazy, Tom. And I don't appreciate being called crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: See? That's exactly what a crazy person would say.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'Dating Mona-Lisa is awesome. Except that I live in constant fear for my life. So I guess it's time to do the mature thing and have someone else dump her for me.'
jokes.setup: Tom reflects on his relationship with Mona-Lisa
jokes.punchline: The 'mature thing' is revealed to be having someone else do it for him — completely undermining the setup of maturity
jokes.explanation: The 'mature thing' setup/subversion is a well-worn structure, but Tom's specific cowardice and the logic of hiring a proxy makes it character-specific. The misdirection ('do the mature thing') earns the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. I will prove to you that Mona-Lisa is crazy. Last week, she tried to fix her car engine with a hammer. A hammer! And when I asked her why, she said, 'Because the screwdriver was tired.' The screwdriver was tired, you guys. A tool cannot be tired. It's a tool.

jokes.text: You said that about every girl you date. You said that about me. / Calm down, Ann. You're proving my point.
jokes.setup: Tom says Mona-Lisa is 'legit insane'
jokes.punchline: Ann points out he said that about her; Tom tells her to calm down — which is instantly self-proving that he does this to everyone, and also a terrible thing to say
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedy logic loop: Ann exposes the pattern → Tom tells her to calm down → which proves the pattern is real. The structure is tight and the Tom/Ann history makes it land harder for fans. 'You're proving my point' as a response to Ann's reasonable objection is perfectly insufferable Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That gas station attendant looks exactly like Yasmine Bleeth.

jokes.text: She once jumped out of a moving car to buy a Nicki Minaj poster.
jokes.setup: Tom argues Mona-Lisa is 'legit insane'
jokes.punchline: The specific, vivid anecdote: jumping from a moving vehicle specifically for a Nicki Minaj poster
jokes.explanation: The specificity sells it — it's not just a dangerous act but a disproportionate one triggered by something as mundane as a celebrity poster. The Nicki Minaj detail makes it funnier than a generic dangerous act would be.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to keep things light and upbeat, like a life raft full of dead bodies.

jokes.text: I'll give you that chenille blanket of mine you love so much. / Deal. / Ugh, but that's my favorite blankie.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ann to break up with Mona-Lisa for him
jokes.punchline: Ann refuses, then immediately accepts for a blanket — and Tom's instant regret ('my favorite blankie') reveals how much he wanted Ann to say no
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure: refusal → instant capitulation for blanket → Tom's buyer's remorse. The word 'blankie' from a grown man makes it funnier. Sets up a running subplot payoff with the blanket.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, that was disgusting. But I'll take it.

jokes.text: I can be a sort of... Conversational lubricant. / Yeah, there's probably a less gross way to say it, but sure.
jokes.setup: Chris offers to help Leslie win over Jamm at mini-golf
jokes.punchline: 'Conversational lubricant' is technically apt but deeply uncomfortable; Leslie acknowledges this with perfect dry deadpan
jokes.explanation: Chris's relentless positivity extends to coining the most unfortunate phrase for his role. Leslie's reaction — acknowledging the grossness without dwelling on it — is pitch-perfect. The joke works because both characters are exactly themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I believe in always being supportive and encouraging. If someone wants to start a business, I say go for it! If someone wants to learn an instrument, I say absolutely! If someone wants to pursue their dreams, I say yes you can!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: If a duck wants to be a astronaut, I say reach for the stars, buddy.

jokes.text: Chris as 'caddy' talking head: enthusiastically describing his philosophy of caddying extended to everyone in his life, with examples: 'Good one! Nice shot! Great sweeping. Way to be, duck.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains he considers himself a 'caddy to everyone in his life'
jokes.punchline: The examples escalate absurdly: encouraging a colleague → 'great sweeping' (janitorial) → 'Way to be, duck' (an actual duck)
jokes.explanation: 'Way to be, duck' is the peak — Chris Traeger's relentless positivity extended to a waterfowl. The escalation to non-human recipients is perfectly absurd and completely consistent with the character.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Thanks, I love this putter. Got it at a great price.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Actually, I stole it from a Chinese guy at the club. He was so small and quiet, I just walked right out with it.

jokes.text: Some fat Hawaiian guy left it in my waiting room. When he came back, I was all like, 'Oh, uh, yeah, yeah, no, I haven't seen it. I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Leslie compliments Jamm's putter
jokes.punchline: Jamm casually reveals he stole it from a patient/visitor using a thin lie, delivered as an amusing anecdote
jokes.explanation: Jamm telling this story as though it's charming is perfect villain comedy. The specificity ('fat Hawaiian guy') and his re-enactment of the lie ('Oh, uh, yeah, yeah, no') makes it vivid. He's proud of this. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Can I offer you a hot dog?

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: No, I can't. I have a very severe hot dog allergy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I didn't know that.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's a real thing. And honestly, I find it pretty racist that you offered it to me.

jokes.text: What a great and funny story.
jokes.setup: Jamm has just cheerfully described stealing a putter from someone
jokes.punchline: Chris, the designated cheerleader, robotically completes his function — calling a story about theft 'great and funny'
jokes.explanation: The joke is Chris's total positivity deployed in the most inappropriate context. It's both a reaction beat and ironic — the audience knows he's just playing his 'caddy' role regardless of content. Economy is the strength.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been thinking about this, and I need to say something. Everyone at work has been talking about how amazing Mouse Rat is. They think we're incredible.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No one said that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: They absolutely did. Ben said our last show was 'life-changing.' Jerry called us 'the voice of a generation.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that didn't happen.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And Chris said he's never heard anything more beautiful than our rendition of 'Catch Your Illness.'

jokes.text: Hot dogs? You know I have irritable bowel syndrome, you racist.
jokes.setup: Leslie offers hot dogs before the round starts
jokes.punchline: 'You racist.' The IBS is an odd but plausible complaint; calling the hot dog offer racist is a non-sequitur that implies Jamm's digestion is somehow a civil rights issue
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The accusation of racism directed at a hot dog offer is completely unhinged and perfectly Jamm. The logic — his IBS is a protected characteristic? Hot dogs are targeted at his ethnicity? — is gloriously unparseable. The 'you racist' lands like a grenade because it's so unexpected and yet so perfectly delivered. Economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable and big room reaction guaranteed.

jokes.text: Ron arrives at the putt-putt and announces he's not playing, just reminding Jamm it costs taxpayers thousands. / 'And what a bargain. I mean, kids love it, adults love it, Jamm loves it. Everybody loves it. It's like the Toy Story 3 of places.'
jokes.setup: Ron attempts to undermine Leslie's case by citing cost
jokes.punchline: Leslie's rebuttal escalates to 'It's like the Toy Story 3 of places' — invoking a beloved but emotionally devastating children's film as a compliment for a putt-putt
jokes.explanation: Toy Story 3 is an inspired reference — it's the movie that made adults cry about their childhood. Leslie's use of it as a compliment for mini-golf is gloriously mismatched in scale. Character-specific Leslie hyperbole.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, so the band couldn't reach me because I got my head stuck in a mailbox.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: How did you get your head stuck in a mailbox?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I was trying to mail a letter, but I wanted to see where it goes, so I stuck my head in to follow it down.

jokes.text: She's buying you snow cones, and tomorrow you're voting on an issue that she cares about. / Hey, guys, what, are we gonna stand around all day and listen to Ron spout off unrelated facts about blah, blah, blah, or are we gonna play?
jokes.setup: Ron tries to point out Leslie is essentially bribing Jamm
jokes.punchline: Jamm summarizes Ron's entire anti-corruption speech as 'blah, blah, blah' and pivots to playing — Jamm is literally the last person to care about political ethics
jokes.explanation: Ron's most principled speech being dismissed as 'blah blah blah' by the episode's most amoral character is darkly funny. Jamm accidentally makes a good point (Ron often is moralizing) while being completely corrupt himself.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about 'Scarecrow Boat'? That's a terrible band name.

dialogue.speaker: Band Member 1
dialogue.line: Actually, that's pretty cool.

dialogue.speaker: Band Member 2
dialogue.line: Yeah, we like that. You're really good at this.

jokes.text: First of all, your nachos are terrible. No one's had the guts to tell you. Why don't you melt the cheese?
jokes.setup: Andy mentions he's the 'nacho chef' of the band
jokes.punchline: Burly has apparently been waiting to say this: no one told Andy his nachos were bad, and the specific critique (unmelted cheese) is both trivial and scathing
jokes.explanation: The callback to nachos lands well. The specificity of 'why don't you melt the cheese?' as a critique of Andy's nachos is funny because it's so small and yet clearly a long-held grievance. 'No one's had the guts to tell you' makes Burly a coward about this specific thing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll have a Bud Light.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: That'll be $5.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? You should really consider expanding your beer selection. Diversify your inventory, build customer loyalty. Trust me, I know business.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody, great news. They gave us free mylar balloons. I got dibs on the dinosaur. / And the pirate and the dolphin. I want all of 'em. / You got 'em. / Sweet.
jokes.setup: Chris announces free mylar balloons at the putt-putt
jokes.punchline: Jamm immediately claims all three balloons with complete seriousness; Chris gives them all up without hesitation
jokes.explanation: A lovely character beat — Jamm's greed is childish and specific (he wants all three), and Chris's immediate capitulation shows his 'caddy' servility. Small but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, whatever. You guys are like my parents arguing about money at mini-golf.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, I think it's great they're so passionate about fiscal responsibility and individual liberty. That's what makes America work.

jokes.text: Andy confronts Burly at the bar: 'I was just over at the bar, enjoying a wonderful night with my co-workers who all talked about how awesome I was, and I look up, and what do I see? A band. But you're missing something like, uh, I don't know, your lead singer/songwriter/T-shirt designer/nacho chef.'
jokes.setup: Andy confronts his bandmates for performing without him
jokes.punchline: His list of self-described roles escalates from legitimate (lead singer, songwriter) to odd (T-shirt designer) to absurd (nacho chef) — and his false modesty setup ('I don't know') makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The escalating job titles — especially 'nacho chef' as a band role — are pure Andy. The false modesty setup ('I don't know') before listing four self-aggrandizing titles is perfect comic irony. This also plants the nacho callback.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ann Perkins.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: If you ever talk to me again, I will kill you.

jokes.text: Well, I dropped my cell phone in a bowl of cereal last week, you idiot. You bothered to call me, you'd have known that.
jokes.setup: Burly says he called Andy's cell 20 times to tell him about the show
jokes.punchline: Andy's phone is in a bowl of cereal. This is delivered as if it's Burly's fault for not knowing.
jokes.explanation: The phone-in-cereal detail is perfectly Andy — not just dropping his phone in liquid (common enough) but specifically a BOWL OF CEREAL (inexplicable). And then blaming Burly for not knowing. The logic is backwards and pure Andy: calling him would have revealed the problem that prevented calling him. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: So what's the deal with Tom? You guys dating or something?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, we're just friends.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Oh. Well I've been trying to steal from him. He's so dumb, it's easy.

jokes.text: Maybe you should change your name to Burly and The Backstabbers. / That's a pretty good name, actually. / Yeah, he's really good at coming up with names.
jokes.setup: Andy insults his band by suggesting they rename themselves 'Burly and the Backstabbers'
jokes.punchline: April and Ben immediately evaluate it as a band name — deflating Andy's dramatic outburst with genuine appreciation for the name
jokes.explanation: A perfect comedic deflation. Andy delivers 'Burly and the Backstabbers' as a devastating insult; his friends miss the emotional register entirely and admire the name. 'Yeah, he's really good at coming up with names' is a lovely callback to Mouse Rat's absurdist naming tradition. The structure — dramatic setup → mundane evaluation → earnest compliment — is extremely well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Wait, Tom has Diddy Instagram coasters? Oh my God, that's so cool. Why doesn't anyone ever buy me cool stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: You know what, forget it. I'm done. I'm going on Instagram right now and I'm going to leave the meanest comments on every celebrity's post.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Hey Beyoncé! Your last album was mid! And Rihanna, where's album number nine?!

jokes.text: Get me a Budweiser Black Crown. You guys got Black Crown here? If not, you should.
jokes.setup: Andy attempts to recover his composure after his burn was co-opted
jokes.punchline: He pivots to ordering beer with the confidence of a man who has strong opinions about beer brands while standing in a dive bar — the 'if not, you should' is overbearing
jokes.explanation: A minor character beat. Andy's confident beer ordering as emotional recovery is a light touch, but not a strong joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy's music taste is so weird. He listens to things like witch house, vaporwave, and seapunk. But then his favorite artist is Bette Midler.

jokes.text: I have two important pieces of caddy information. Councilman Jamm leads by eight strokes, and you are both about to set a course record. / For friendship.
jokes.setup: Chris announces the score
jokes.punchline: After 'you are both about to set a course record,' the follow-up 'For friendship' reveals it's not a real golf record — and the pause makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Chris's endless positivity finds a workaround for bad news — they're terrible at golf but great friends. The beat before 'For friendship' is the structural key. Warm and funny.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why do you have a computer fan on this list?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because computers get hot, April. They need fans to cool down. It's science.

jokes.text: You are pandering to get a vote. And worse, you're deliberately losing. / I am not deliberately losing. I'm having a very off night.
jokes.setup: Ron accuses Leslie of throwing the game to flatter Jamm
jokes.punchline: Leslie's denial ('I'm having a very off night') is transparently false and she knows it
jokes.explanation: A workmanlike joke that's elevated by Leslie's transparent dishonesty. 'Very off night' at miniature golf is a nice touch of absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Tom's not poor. He's just financially challenged.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa, he drinks tap water straight from the sink.

jokes.text: Losing on purpose is a form of lying. You're only as good as your word.
jokes.setup: Leslie defends her strategy of letting Jamm win
jokes.punchline: Ron applies his rigid philosophical code to mini-golf — treating a casual putt-putt game with the gravity of a solemn oath
jokes.explanation: Ron's absolute moral code applied to mini-golf is funny because he means it completely. 'You're only as good as your word' as a response to someone sandbagging a round of putt-putt is perfect Ron Swanson. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Tom is broke? That's so sad. I guess he'll have to start doing poor people things now, like shopping at regular stores and eating at Applebee's.

jokes.text: I will do anything I can to get Jamm's vote so that he will keep this course open, and it will be good for the community-- stop! I know it's more than one word. Shut up.
jokes.setup: Ron says 'You want a word, Ron?' — clearly intending a single-word answer; Leslie launches into a full speech
jokes.punchline: Ron preemptively corrects himself ('Stop! I know it's more than one word. Shut up.') — catching his own error before anyone else can
jokes.explanation: Ron self-correcting ('I know it's more than one word. Shut up.') is a great beat — his pride prevents him from letting anyone else point out his error. The joke rewards attention to the setup. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Ann introduces herself to Mona-Lisa: 'I'm Ann Perkins. I used to date Tom.' / 'Oh, okay. We can do this, but I will bite you.'
jokes.setup: Ann approaches Mona-Lisa to have a 'woman-to-woman' conversation
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa interprets the meeting as a potential fight and immediately warns she will bite
jokes.explanation: 'I will bite you' as a pre-emptive negotiating position is gloriously unhinged. The specificity of biting (not punching, not anything normal) and the matter-of-fact delivery is what makes it. Mona-Lisa's casual threat perfectly characterizes her chaos energy. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Do you know his ATM pin? 'Cause I cannot crack that little bitch's code.
jokes.setup: Ann says she knows Tom well
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's immediate pivot is to try to get Tom's bank PIN — this is her conception of 'knowing someone well'
jokes.explanation: Mona-Lisa treats intimacy as financial access — 'knowing someone' means having their PIN. 'That little bitch's code' is a great phrase. The joke efficiently reveals her as both financially predatory and oddly frustrated by Tom. Strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, my time in the Sweetums was amazing. We played Ramsett's that one time, and I made these nachos with, like, Cheeto dust and spray cheese. Everyone said they were terrible, but I thought they were incredible. I really did.

jokes.text: You know what used to drive me nuts? He is a total control freak. I mean, you have to put a coaster down on every surface, and the worst part is, they're all made out of pictures from Diddy's Instagram.
jokes.setup: Ann is pretending to bond with Mona-Lisa over Tom's flaws
jokes.punchline: The absurd specificity: coasters from Diddy's Instagram — not just branded merchandise but something Tom specifically made from social media screenshots
jokes.explanation: The Diddy Instagram coasters are a perfect Tom Haverford detail — they imply he's obsessively into Diddy, that he makes his own decor, and that he's deeply particular about coasters. It's a detail rich enough to fuel a whole spinoff. High originality and character integration because it's uniquely Tom-specific.

jokes.text: Diddy's on Instagram? How did I not know that Diddy was on Instagram, you jagweeds? / Who are you yelling at? / The jagweeds.
jokes.setup: Ann mentions Diddy's Instagram
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa yells at unseen people ('jagweeds') for not telling her about Diddy's Instagram; when asked who she's yelling at, she identifies them as 'the jagweeds'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. Mona-Lisa yelling at invisible people, calling them 'jagweeds,' and when asked who she's yelling at, simply confirming 'the jagweeds' — it's absurdist and completely self-contained in its own perfect logic. The word 'jagweeds' is inspired. The follow-up 'Why are you still in front of me?' to Ann is a bonus beat. Mona-Lisa operates on her own reality and this scene captures it perfectly. Near-perfect economy. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Anna Nicole body spray? That's what you're using?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What's wrong with it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, that stuff is basically just desperation in a bottle.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Actually, I've been diluting old perfume with gross additives to stretch it out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what additives?

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Well, there's some old lotion, a little bit of coconut oil, and honestly, I'm not sure what that last one is.

jokes.text: Why are you still in front of me?
jokes.setup: Ann is standing there after Mona-Lisa's jagweeds outburst
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa treats Ann's continued presence as a personal affront — she's done with Ann mid-conversation
jokes.explanation: A bonus beat from the jagweeds joke. Mona-Lisa's dismissal is cold and funny — she's completely checked out of this interaction. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would they put a windmill in front of the hole? That seems like poor course design.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I'm done with that band. I mean, I'm an adult now, you know? I work two part-time jobs. Hello. I don't need the stress of playing guitar with my friends every few weeks.'
jokes.setup: Andy declares he's done with Mouse Rat
jokes.punchline: His evidence of adulthood is 'two part-time jobs' (not a full-time job) and the 'stress' of playing guitar occasionally — the bar for adulthood and stress is hilariously low
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'I'm an adult' confessional is a Parks classic structure. The specifics are perfect: two PART-TIME jobs as proof of maturity, and 'every few weeks' exposing how low-stakes his 'stress' is. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, Ron! Hey, Ron! Did you know that the government actually does a lot of good things? Libraries! Parks! Public education!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And did you hear about that article that came out saying that John Locke, your hero, actually believed in some forms of taxation?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're trying to distract me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is it working?

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'I love Andy, but to be perfectly honest, Mouse Rat's music is not my thing. I really only listen to, like, German Death Reggae and Halloween sound effects records from the 1950s. And Bette Midler. Obviously.'
jokes.setup: April discusses Andy's music
jokes.punchline: German Death Reggae → 1950s Halloween records → 'And Bette Midler. Obviously.' — the escalating darkness/weirdness followed by the completely sincere, totally incongruous Bette Midler confession
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The structure is flawless: German Death Reggae establishes April's gothic credentials, 1950s Halloween records doubles down, and then 'Bette Midler. Obviously.' is the perfect subversion — delivered with complete sincerity and the word 'obviously' implying that of course this follows logically. The 'obviously' is the key word that elevates it from funny to brilliant. Extremely quotable. Strong rewatch value. Only April Ludgate could deliver this line — it's perfectly character-integrated. Rivals the anchor examples for structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: What in the name of all that is holy and sacred, and all that is unholy and profane, in this mortal coil of existence, is occurring before my very eyes?

jokes.text: Andy announces his 'monster farewell performance solo' on stage, then lists requirements: 'I need a piece of paper, I need a pen, I need four more beers, I need a computer fan, I need a lightning bolt of inspiration. It's song writing time.'
jokes.setup: Andy decides to do a farewell solo performance
jokes.punchline: The list of requirements escalates from sensible (paper, pen) to odd (four more beers) to completely inexplicable (a computer fan)
jokes.explanation: The computer fan is the peak — its presence in a songwriting supply list demands explanation, which Andy then provides in joke #46. The escalation of the requirements list is good Andy chaos energy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: So you two are together? That's great. Hey, I know a guy who needs a kidney. You should call him.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, we're not—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We're not actually—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, how much is he paying?

jokes.text: What do you need a computer fan for? / Sometimes when you use a computer, it gets hot, and the fan cools it down.
jokes.setup: April asks why Andy needs a computer fan to write a song
jokes.punchline: Andy explains what a computer fan DOES, not why he NEEDS one — a perfect Andy non-answer delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Andy joke. He answers a 'why' question with a 'what' answer — not deceptively, but because his brain genuinely couldn't distinguish between the two questions. The explanation is technically correct and completely unhelpful. Strong character integration: only Andy would give this answer with full confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm finally free from Mona-Lisa! This is the best day of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, you were only dating her for like two weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. Two weeks of pure hell. I deserve a parade.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head-adjacent exchange: 'You know, I think it's great that you're cool with Tom's financial situation.' / 'What are you talking about? Tommy owns his own business.'
jokes.setup: Ann is manipulating Mona-Lisa by implying Tom is broke
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa has no idea Tom has financial problems — she thought his business made him rich
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the Tom-break-up plot. The comedy is in the gap between Mona-Lisa's assumption and reality. Not highly original but well-structured as a plot-comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm a completely different person now. The old Andy Dwyer? He's dead. Gone. I've shed my skin like a snake made of idiocy and poor life choices. I'm reborn as a phoenix of competence and professionalism.

jokes.text: Tom drinks tap water. / What? [then confronting Tom:] You're broke? / Mm, yeah, super broke. Are you upset about that? / Mm, yeah, 'cause I don't eff with poorsies.
jokes.setup: Ann reveals Tom's poverty by saying 'he drinks tap water'
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's euphemism for poor people: 'poorsies' — and her policy of not 'effing with' them
jokes.explanation: 'Poorsies' is an inspired coinage — it's the word a terrible person would invent to make themselves feel better about financial discrimination. 'I don't eff with poorsies' is both a policy statement and an accidental self-own. 'Tap water' as the damning evidence of poverty is also great — the specificity of the social signifier. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, focusing on business is great because it really streamlines your priorities and helps you achieve your goals.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But the real reason I do it is so I have more time for childish pursuits.

jokes.text: And I don't even usually like Puerto Rican chicks. / I'm not -- I mean, it shouldn't matter, but I'm--
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is trying to compliment Ann as she ends her involvement with Tom
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's 'compliment' is racist; Ann's response is perfectly calibrated — starting to correct her race, then stopping because she's right it shouldn't matter
jokes.explanation: Ann's double-take reaction — starting to correct the racial assumption, then realizing she's making a separate point — is a nice bit of character work. Mona-Lisa's oblivious racism-as-compliment is well in character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: How much did you pay for the gorilla?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Three thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Three thousand dollars? For a gorilla?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was worth it to make my point about the importance of animal welfare in our community.

jokes.text: You're breaking up with me? / Oh, man, that sucks. / That's right. It's over. Let's go dance. / Help.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa announces she's breaking up with Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'Oh, man, that sucks' is performed for Ann but hollow; Mona-Lisa immediately pivots to 'Let's go dance'; Tom's final plaintive 'Help.' is the button
jokes.explanation: Tom's single-word 'Help.' is the best beat — he got what he wanted (a breakup) and is now confused by Mona-Lisa's chaos continuing. The word 'Help.' as a complete sentence, delivered to no one in particular, is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll name him Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no! His name is Mittens!

jokes.text: It's getting late, and Jeremy's eaten all the syrup.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to dismiss the snow cone vendor
jokes.punchline: The reason she gives: Jamm has eaten all the syrup — not the snow cones, but specifically the syrup
jokes.explanation: Eating 'all the syrup' implies Jamm has been consuming it in an unusually gluttonous way (not just snow cones but the raw syrup itself). The specificity is what makes it — it's a minor visual gag that characterizes Jamm as an id-driven creature.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We have a gorilla that needs to be catalogued. The official designation is Gorilla Specimen 47-B.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we're naming him Gerald. Look at his little face! Gerald is going to be my best friend.

jokes.text: Snow cones are half the fun. / Yeah, Julie, could you stay, please? / I have calculus homework. I-- / Oh, well, math is worthless in real life. I mean, there's an app for calculating tips. That's all you need.
jokes.setup: Julie the snow cone vendor wants to go home for homework
jokes.punchline: Jamm dismisses calculus as worthless and says a tip calculator app is all you need from math
jokes.explanation: Jamm the orthodontist who uses science daily dismissing math to a student is appropriately ironic and terrible. The tip app as the ceiling of mathematical need is an inspired specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So how was your night with Mona-Lisa?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, it was great. We went to dinner, had some drinks, told some stories.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then we went back to her place and committed several federal crimes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Nothing major, just some light wire fraud, tax evasion, and we may have stolen a car.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, not stole it. We borrowed it. Without permission. From a dealership. At 3 AM. And sold it for parts.

jokes.text: Math is very important, especially for young women. Stay in school.
jokes.setup: Jamm has told Julie that math is worthless
jokes.punchline: Leslie counter-programs with earnest pro-education messaging — she can't help being wholesome even while trying to secure a corrupt vote
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's inability to suppress her earnest civic goodness even in a corrupt moment. Functional character comedy — not sharp but true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: She started with petty theft, then moved to grand larceny, then drug fraud. She was selling counterfeit Goldschläger at a gas station in Gary, Indiana.

jokes.text: I've made my point. Leslie has made hers. Which way are you voting, Councilman? / Uh, well, I'm kind of still on the fence about this budget thing, but I do love watching you guys squabble over me. You sure make a guy feel like a real lady.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Jamm directly which way he's voting
jokes.punchline: 'You sure make a guy feel like a real lady.' — Jamm's non-answer is a bizarre compliment about feeling desired
jokes.explanation: Jamm's 'feel like a real lady' is a strange, self-satisfied phrase that's funny precisely because it's unclear what he means — he's enjoying being courted, and expresses it in the weirdest possible way. Consistent Jamm weirdness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You gave Ron your word.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, my word doesn't mean anything. I lie constantly. I'm not a man of my word at all.

jokes.text: Sudden death playoff on the very course that hangs in the balance. / I could literally faint if I didn't have impeccable blood pressure.
jokes.setup: Ron proposes a sudden death playoff for Jamm's vote
jokes.punchline: Leslie says she 'could literally faint' then immediately undermines the drama by noting her impeccable blood pressure prevents it
jokes.explanation: One of the better jokes in the episode. The structure is ideal: Leslie builds to a dramatic statement ('I could literally faint') then deflates it with a medically specific qualifier ('if I didn't have impeccable blood pressure'). The word 'impeccable' is perfectly Leslie — she's proud of her health stats even in a tense moment. High economy and structure scores justified.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Ron, here's the situation. One: we need to shut down the park. Two: we can't shut down the park. Three: we're going to shut down the park anyway. Four: I love this town and I will die protecting it.

jokes.text: Andy's announcement monologue: 'My name is Andy Dwyer. You probably know me as the artist formerly known as the lead singer of Mouse Rat. Well, after tonight, you'll only know me as the former artist formerly known as the lead singer of Mouse Rat. I'm retiring from music. This is my swan song.'
jokes.setup: Andy takes the stage for his farewell performance
jokes.punchline: 'Former artist formerly known as the lead singer of Mouse Rat' — a pun/riff on 'the artist formerly known as Prince' that creates a grammatically absurd but logical chain
jokes.explanation: The Prince reference riff is well-constructed — 'former artist formerly known as' is a genuinely clever doubling that maintains internal logic while becoming absurd. Andy's earnest delivery makes it land. The pause before 'I'm retiring from music' as a dramatic reveal is good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I think the ideal political discourse is when two people with different viewpoints can sit down, listen to each other, and find common ground.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I disagree.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But honestly? I usually win our arguments by like 3 p.m. because you get hungry and I've already eaten lunch.

jokes.text: Andy's swan song lyrics: '♪ Once I was a golden swan / Swan of a man / Now that swan's name was Andy / And he started a rock and roll band / He made incredible nachos / That everybody claimed they loved / And then the bandmates dicked him over / With a massive rock and roll shove ♪'
jokes.setup: Andy performs his farewell 'swan song'
jokes.punchline: The lyrics blend sincere emotionality with absurdity ('swan of a man') and specific grievance ('incredible nachos that everybody claimed they loved' — implying they didn't really love them, and 'dicked him over with a massive rock and roll shove')
jokes.explanation: The swan song lyrics are genuinely clever. 'Swan of a man' is beautiful/absurd. The nacho callback ('claimed they loved' — not 'loved') is a subtle dig that implies Andy knew they were lying. 'Dicked him over with a massive rock and roll shove' is a great phrasing. Strong character integration because these are exactly Andy's petty grievances elevated to myth.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been in bands with two lead vocalists before. It works great.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The Beatles.

jokes.text: Why is there a gorilla guarding this gingerbread house? — Because mini-golf is awesome. It's cute, and it's fun, and it needs to be saved. — Less talk. More competing for my vote.
jokes.setup: The group arrives at a mini-golf hole featuring a gorilla and a gingerbread house
jokes.punchline: Ron's genuine architectural confusion about the decor is answered by Leslie's non-answer; Jamm cuts through both of them
jokes.explanation: The visual of a gorilla guarding a gingerbread house is inherently absurdist, and the joke is that nobody finds this worth explaining. Ron's genuine question vs. Leslie's non-answer is a nice character beat. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

jokes.text: Why is there a gorilla guarding this gingerbread house? / Because mini-golf is awesome. It's cute, and it's fun, and it needs to be saved.
jokes.setup: They arrive at a hole featuring a gorilla and a gingerbread house
jokes.punchline: Leslie treats the absurd putt-putt decor as a completely valid reason to fight for the course
jokes.explanation: Ron's confused straight-man question about the mini-golf design is good, and Leslie's defense ('because mini-golf is awesome') is perfectly circular. The visual absurdity of a gorilla guarding a gingerbread house is implied and funny.

jokes.text: Uh, bean sprouts. Tofu. Ralph Nader. Ayn Rand is a terrible writer. Don't mess up, don't mess up, don't mess up.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to attempt a hole-in-one that would win Jamm's vote
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to distract Ron with things he hates — health food, a political figure, an intellectual hero — the Ayn Rand jab is the peak because it's the most targeted to Ron specifically
jokes.explanation: Leslie's psych-out list is a brilliant character piece. It escalates from food items Ron dislikes (bean sprouts, tofu) to political figures (Ralph Nader) to the coup de grâce: 'Ayn Rand is a terrible writer' — targeting Ron's philosophical idol. The list is a perfect inventory of Leslie's knowledge of Ron's triggers. 'Don't mess up, don't mess up, don't mess up' as a whispered self-reminder caps it beautifully. High character integration for both characters — Leslie knows Ron precisely.

jokes.text: Damn it! / Hole-in-one! [Ron wins the playoff]
jokes.setup: Ron attempts the decisive shot while Leslie tries to distract him
jokes.punchline: Despite all the distractions, Ron makes the hole-in-one — a visual comedy beat where the psych-out fails completely
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the psych-out sequence. Ron's total imperviousness to Leslie's attempts makes both characters funnier — her desperation and his implacable skill. The comedy is in the implied physical moment.

jokes.text: Excellent win, Ron. Even better loss, Leslie. Ultimately, we learn the most about ourselves through the losses.
jokes.setup: Ron wins the playoff
jokes.punchline: Chris congratulates both parties equally — 'even better loss' implies losing is actually superior, which is absurd positivity applied to defeat
jokes.explanation: 'Even better loss' is a great phrase — Chris's positivity so extreme it inverts the value of winning and losing. His follow-up platitude is robotic optimism at its most absurd.

jokes.text: Swanson, I hate you. Nothing will change that. But I respect the hell out of your short game. You got my vote, hombre.
jokes.setup: Ron wins the playoff
jokes.punchline: Jamm's endorsement structure — personal hatred + profound golf respect → vote — is absurd logic taken seriously, capped with 'hombre'
jokes.explanation: Jamm's civic philosophy reduced to: who has the better short game at putt-putt. 'Hombre' as a send-off is a nice weird touch. The structure of 'I hate you... but I respect your golf' is a funny inversion of how endorsements work.

jokes.text: No, he gets the dragon too? — A fine trophy. — I think I'll keep it in the office. — No, you won't. — Here, kid, want this, huh? — Yeah. — Take it and run. Run!
jokes.setup: Ron wins a plastic dragon trophy for getting a hole-in-one on 18
jokes.punchline: Leslie's outrage at him getting the dragon leads Ron to give it to a random child with the directive 'Take it and run. Run!' — thwarting Leslie's attempt to claim it
jokes.explanation: 'Take it and run. Run!' is a great Ron Swanson line — the urgency implies Leslie is a genuine threat to the child's balloon animal dragon. The visual of a child sprinting away from Leslie Knope with a dragon is inherently funny.

jokes.text: You get a hole-in-one on 18, so I'm supposed to give you this. [trophy] / No, he gets the dragon too? / A fine trophy. I think I'll keep it in the office. / No, you won't. / Here, kid, want this, huh? / Yeah. / Take it and run. Run!
jokes.setup: Ron wins a trophy dragon for his hole-in-one
jokes.punchline: Ron tries to keep the trophy; Leslie objects; Ron immediately gives it to a child and tells them to run — prioritizing denying Leslie over keeping the trophy himself
jokes.explanation: Ron's strategic trophy redistribution — giving it to a child specifically to prevent Leslie from having it, then telling the child to 'Run!' — is a great physical comedy bit. It reveals Ron would rather a stranger have it than concede to Leslie. 'Run!' is the perfect button.

jokes.text: What the mother-effing, c-ing ess-ing, effing k-ing eff is going on right now?
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa finds Tom and Ann together
jokes.punchline: Her profanity is so extreme she has to spell/abbreviate it — the censored string is funny as a catalog of expletives and for how long it goes
jokes.explanation: The escalating censored profanity is funny in its absurd length and the effort to decode it. Mona-Lisa's visceral reaction to what is a fairly mundane betrayal is consistent with her chaos energy.

jokes.text: Sorry, Mona-Lisa. We can't keep our hands off each other. / That is accurate.
jokes.setup: Tom claims he and Ann are an item to make Mona-Lisa jealous/confused
jokes.punchline: Ann's flat 'That is accurate' — she's playing along but her robot-like delivery undercuts the romantic claim
jokes.explanation: 'That is accurate' as a romantic affirmation is a perfectly Ann-robotic line — she's trying to lie but produces something clinically truthful-sounding. Short and clean.

jokes.text: You guys want a threesome. / What? No. We do not wanna have a threesome with you. / Well, let's not rush to judgment. I mean, I say we hear her out.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa processes Ann and Tom acting like a couple
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'let's not rush to judgment. I say we hear her out' — he's genuinely considering the threesome offer that Ann immediately shut down
jokes.explanation: Tom's measured consideration of the threesome offer — using deliberative language ('let's not rush to judgment', 'hear her out') as if it's a board meeting proposal — is both gross and hilarious. It's perfectly Tom. Ann's 'Gross' as a one-word veto is the correct reaction and a good button.

jokes.text: Look, I still don't think we should date. / Oh, me neither. I've been single for an hour now, and it's the tits!
jokes.setup: The Mona-Lisa situation resolved, Ann and Tom assess their status
jokes.punchline: 'I've been single for an hour now, and it's the tits!' — Tom's enthusiasm for one hour of freedom, expressed with characteristic swagger
jokes.explanation: 'It's the tits' after one hour of singledom is great Tom Haverford energy — maximum enthusiasm, minimum time elapsed. The specificity of 'an hour' grounds the absurdity.

jokes.text: I'd still like to hook up though. / Yo, do you wanna have a threesome with us? [to Mona-Lisa] / Yeah, okay. / Cool. All right. / Sweet. All right.
jokes.setup: Tom wants to hook up with Ann anyway; she's starting to consider it; Mona-Lisa is right there
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately pivots to asking Mona-Lisa about a threesome — and everyone agrees with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: The callback to the threesome offer pays off — what was outrageous before is now casual. The flat, businesslike 'Yeah, okay. / Cool. All right. / Sweet. All right.' exchanges are funny in their complete normalization of something absurd.

jokes.text: I'd still like to hook up though. — Yo, do you wanna have a threesome with us? — Yeah, okay. — Cool. All right. — Sweet. All right. — Yo, what up? My name is Mona-Lisa.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann have agreed to not date each other; Mona-Lisa invites a random stranger to a threesome
jokes.punchline: The stranger immediately agrees ('Yeah, okay') with zero hesitation; Mona-Lisa's introduction 'Yo, what up? My name is Mona-Lisa' comes AFTER the threesome is arranged
jokes.explanation: The stranger's immediate 'Yeah, okay' gets the first laugh, but the real joke is Mona-Lisa introducing herself AFTER everything has been arranged — introductions are an afterthought to logistics. The 'Cool. All right. / Sweet. All right.' rhythm between Tom and the stranger is a funny detail too.

jokes.text: Well, hello, fellow employees. Co-workers, I bid you adieu. Whoa, fancy Andy. — Oh, me? No. This is just how I dress now.
jokes.setup: Andy returns to the office in a suit after his retirement performance
jokes.punchline: April calls him 'fancy Andy' and he immediately denies it's a costume — 'this is just how I dress now' — committing fully to his new business persona
jokes.explanation: The visual of Andy in a suit is inherently funny given the character, and 'this is just how I dress now' is his all-in commitment to a persona he adopted approximately last night. Good visual gag with strong character integration.

jokes.text: Well, hello, fellow employees. Co-workers, I bid you adieu. / Whoa, fancy Andy. / Oh, me? No. This is just how I dress now.
jokes.setup: Andy returns after his swan song, now dressed formally
jokes.punchline: 'This is just how I dress now' — Andy has fully committed to a new personality with zero transition time
jokes.explanation: Andy's instant persona transformation — formal wear, affected speech ('I bid you adieu') — and his deadpan 'this is just how I dress now' is great. He commits 100% immediately. Strong Andy character integration.

jokes.text: Funny goofball music Andy... Is gone. You're left with the professional remains. I'm an adult now. I'm gonna focus on business, which is good. Give me more time to play video games.
jokes.setup: Andy declares his transformation to 'professional'
jokes.punchline: The benefit of business focus: 'more time to play video games' — completely undermining the maturity thesis
jokes.explanation: 'Professional remains' is a nice phrase, but the real punchline — business focus will free up video game time — is perfectly Andy. He genuinely doesn't see the contradiction. 'Which is good' as a self-reassurance is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Why, so they can steal my swan song? Ha, joke's on them. I forgot it.
jokes.setup: April tells Andy to call Burly and ask to rejoin the band
jokes.punchline: Andy's gloating that the band can't steal his swan song — because he forgot it — immediately after performing it
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully constructed joke. Andy's gloating about the band not being able to steal his swan song, immediately undermined by the revelation he's already forgotten it, is perfect. The confidence of 'joke's on them' leading to 'I forgot it' is a classic misdirection structure. High character integration — only Andy would forget his own farewell song moments after writing and performing it.

jokes.text: Okay, what's in there? / I don't know. / I-it's locked. / Yeah, that's my briefcase. / Is it?
jokes.setup: Andy has a briefcase as part of his new professional identity
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know what's in it, and then isn't sure if it's his — suggesting he acquired a random locked briefcase as a prop for his persona
jokes.explanation: The briefcase joke is quietly great. Andy's 'Is it?' — genuine uncertainty about whether a locked briefcase is his — implies he just grabbed it somewhere. The minimalist exchange achieves a lot. Economy is very strong.

jokes.text: Good gravy. / Oh, hello, Ron. I believe you know this gorilla. It used to bring joy to hundreds of Pawnee families, but then you got rid of its habitat, so it died. Your office shall serve as its monkey tomb.
jokes.setup: Ron returns to his office
jokes.punchline: Leslie has installed the full-size gorilla from the putt-putt in Ron's office and assigned it a tragic backstory: 'Your office shall serve as its monkey tomb'
jokes.explanation: 'Your office shall serve as its monkey tomb' is one of the episode's best lines. Leslie's commitment to the bit — giving the gorilla a full tragic narrative — is Leslie at her most gloriously petty and righteous. 'Monkey tomb' is an inspired coinage. The visual of Ron arriving to find a life-sized gorilla in his office (Ron's 'Good gravy' as reaction) elevates this further. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.text: How much did you pay for this? / Irrelevant. I would pay any amount of money to properly shame you.
jokes.setup: Ron finds a full-size gorilla in his office
jokes.punchline: 'I would pay any amount of money to properly shame you' — Leslie's financial commitment to public humiliation is absolute
jokes.explanation: 'I would pay any amount of money to properly shame you' is a great line — it's both an absurd declaration and completely true for Leslie. The word 'properly' is key: she's not just shaming him, she's doing it properly. Very quotable. Extremely character-specific to Leslie.

jokes.text: I will call him '$9,000 of taxpayer money the gorilla.' / That is a terrible-- his name is Mr. Fuzzyface!
jokes.setup: Ron decides to keep the gorilla but names it after the budget he's proud of cutting
jokes.punchline: Leslie's outraged correction — 'his name is Mr. Fuzzyface!' — reveals she had already named the gorilla, further committing to the bit
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron's bureaucratic full name for the gorilla ('$9,000 of taxpayer money the gorilla') is perfect — he weaponizes the name as a perpetual reminder of his victory. But the real punchline is Leslie's anguished 'his name is Mr. Fuzzyface!' — revealing she'd already given it a warm, fuzzy name, confirming her complete emotional investment in this gorilla. The structural reversal (Ron accepts the gift by destroying its purpose; Leslie reveals she cares more than the shaming warranted) is exquisitely constructed. Near-perfect structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Mona-Lisa eventually threw a cinderblock through the girl's windshield. She dives in, steals her purse, doesn't go for the money, steals all her birth control pills, and says, 'Bitch, you're gonna get pregnant.'
jokes.setup: Tom recounts what happened after Ann left the bar
jokes.punchline: The escalating chaos: windshield → purse → ONLY the birth control → threat of pregnancy as a power move
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes — a masterclass in comedic escalation. Each beat is more insane than the last: violence → theft → selective theft (only birth control) → the verbal threat 'you're gonna get pregnant.' Stealing ONLY the birth control and leaving the money is the brilliant pivot — it implies Mona-Lisa's motivation is reproductive warfare, not financial gain. The threat is simultaneously menacing and absurd. This is dark subversive comedy at a high level. Exceptional structure, originality, and character integration.

jokes.text: She then pretends those are ecstasy and sells it to a bunch of college kids that are drinking Goldschläger at a gas station.
jokes.setup: Continuation of the Mona-Lisa windshield/birth control story
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa sells stolen birth control as ecstasy to Goldschläger-drinking college kids at a gas station — the specificity of Goldschläger and the gas station setting adds layers
jokes.explanation: The Goldschläger detail is the signature touch — it paints an extremely specific portrait of the sad college kids who would be hanging out at a gas station drinking Goldschläger. Mona-Lisa's drug deal capper is a perfect escalation of the story. 'At a gas station' as the setting elevates the whole image. Strong continuation joke.

jokes.text: It did not go well. / Did she assault you? / No, this was a... sexual injury.
jokes.setup: Tom reports that his latest breakup attempt with Mona-Lisa did not go well
jokes.punchline: 'This was a... sexual injury' — the pause before the revelation and Tom's pained admission
jokes.explanation: 'Sexual injury' as a two-word category is excellent. The structure — Ann assumes assault, Tom corrects to something potentially worse — is a clean misdirection. The pause implied before the revelation is key. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Here's your chenille blanket. You earned it. / Thanks for your help. Tom, thank you. / Eh, be nice to Chenille O'Neal. / I will. / It needs to be brushed regularly. Never use a lint roller.
jokes.setup: Tom returns the chenille blanket as payment for Ann's help
jokes.punchline: Tom's care instructions for the blanket escalate into the kind of instructions you'd give for a living pet — 'Chenille O'Neal' as a name, brush regularly, no lint roller
jokes.explanation: The blanket callback pays off with the escalating care instructions. 'Chenille O'Neal' is a great name for a blanket. Tom treating the blanket like a beloved pet reveals how attached he was — making his earlier eagerness to get it back funnier in retrospect.

jokes.text: I'm dead serious. / Okay, you know what, I don't even want it anymore. / Yes! Thank you!
jokes.setup: Tom is giving Ann increasingly intense care instructions for the blanket
jokes.punchline: Ann surrenders the blanket back out of sheer overwhelm; Tom celebrates — he never wanted to give it away
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Tom's master plan — unconsciously or deliberately — was to make the care instructions so annoying that Ann would give up the blanket. His 'Yes! Thank you!' reveals his true feelings about the blanket transaction from the start. The structure pays off the initial 'my favorite blankie' moment beautifully.

jokes.text: A few months ago, you traded me your office for that stupid swimming pool bill. Last night you bring in a teenage girl to pump me full of snow cones.
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses shock at Jamm's sleazy vote-trading offer
jokes.punchline: Jamm lists Leslie's own transgressions to normalize his behavior — including 'pump me full of snow cones' which is both accurate and sounds terrible
jokes.explanation: 'Pump me full of snow cones' is a phrase that shouldn't sound as inappropriate as it does — the verb choice is Jamm's warped framing. The callback to the office trade and the teenage snow cone vendor is well-earned plot comedy.

jokes.text: Ron's numbered list speech to Leslie: '...Four: I am sorry that I said the gorilla's blood was on your hands. 'Twas Leslie killed the beast.'
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Leslie a formal itemized speech about the putt-putt situation
jokes.punchline: 'Twas Leslie killed the beast' — Ron's sudden shift to archaic/literary register, paraphrasing Kong mythology
jokes.explanation: 'Twas Leslie killed the beast' is a great line — Ron's formality and tendency toward dramatic pronouncements collides with the King Kong paraphrase, and the gorilla callback gives it a second layer. The archaic 'Twas' is perfectly Ron. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ron's speech item six: 'Your rigid code of honor, which drives me nuts, makes you a wonderful human being, and I am proud to call you my friend, and don't ever change.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been berating Leslie's methods through five points; item six is the reversal
jokes.punchline: Ron's full emotional reversal — the thing that drives him nuts is what makes her wonderful — delivered in Ron's formal speech-giving register
jokes.explanation: The numbered speech structure makes this payoff land — Ron using an itemized list to deliver a heartfelt compliment is perfectly his character. The joke is the contrast between the formal delivery mechanism and the warm content. Strong character integration: only Ron would express affection through parliamentary procedure.

jokes.text: Frankly, I hoped it would be like dealing with you. People with strong opinions hashing it out respectfully. / And then you either realize that I'm right or you get hungry and go home and I win.
jokes.setup: Leslie says she hoped politics would be like her relationship with Ron — healthy debate
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals his version of 'hashing it out respectfully' ends with him winning because the other person gets hungry and leaves
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes — a masterful Ron line. Ron's description of 'respectful debate' is that he outlasts people until they get hungry and leave, and then he wins. It's simultaneously a critique of himself (he doesn't actually convince people, he just persists), a perfect distillation of his character, and genuinely funny as a strategy. 'Or you get hungry and go home and I win' is an all-time Ron line. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I'm taking that gorilla with me and putting it back in the putt-putt when it reopens. / Sorry, no. That gorilla was a gift from a very determined co-worker whom I respect. And there's a certain code of honor that accompanies gift-giving. / God, you're the worst.
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to reclaim the gorilla for the putt-putt
jokes.punchline: Ron invokes his code of honor to keep the gorilla — the very code Leslie criticized all episode — to specifically deny her the thing she gave him as punishment
jokes.explanation: A superb episode-closing joke. Ron uses his rigid code of honor — which Leslie attacked all episode — to keep the very gorilla she brought to shame him. He weaponizes his own code against her, and the irony is that she can't argue against his principle without arguing against herself. 'God, you're the worst' is the only possible response, and it's perfect. This is a callback to multiple threads (gorilla, code of honor) with a satisfying structural reversal. Excellent craft.

jokes.text: That gorilla was a gift from a very determined co-worker whom I respect. And there's a certain code of honor that accompanies gift-giving. — God, you're the worst.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to reclaim the gorilla for the re-opened putt-putt course
jokes.punchline: Ron invokes his own 'code of honor' — which he's been championing all episode — to keep the gorilla she gave him as a shame gift. Leslie's 'God, you're the worst' is the button.
jokes.explanation: A great callback that uses the episode's thematic argument (code of honor) against Leslie — she gave him the gorilla to shame him, and now he weaponizes the gift-giving code to keep it. Beautifully circular. 'God, you're the worst' is the perfect Leslie button.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Mouse Rat's Reunion Show, featuring me, Andy Dwyer, and for the first time, Andrew 'Burly' Burlinson on lead vocals. That's right, two lead vocalists. Name one other band that's done that. / The Beatles. / Three, four!
jokes.setup: Andy triumphantly announces Mouse Rat's reunion, challenging anyone to name another two-lead-vocalist band
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately names The Beatles; Andy ignores it and counts in the song
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode button. Andy's rhetorical 'name one other band' is immediately answered by Ben (The Beatles), and Andy simply ignores it and starts the song. The economy is excellent — Ben's one-word answer does all the deflating necessary, and Andy's refusal to acknowledge it is funnier than any response would be. Great character work from both: Ben the nerd who knows his rock history, Andy the oblivious optimist.

tmdb_overview: Leslie deems Ron's budget-cut proposals unacceptable. Andy and Ben celebrate a big donation made to their charity. Ann tries to solve Tom's girlfriend troubles.
insight: Solid character work carries an otherwise uneven episode with 61 jokes across 22 minutes.
